lead: A thin wall carries direct stress almost evenly across its thickness. That lets you replace a real wing or fuselage section with a few concentrated boom areas at corners and thin walls between them. Area and second moments then become simple bookkeeping. This chapter shows the thin-wall assumption, the boom-plus-wall idealisation, the half-wall rule, and the section properties I_xx, I_yy and I_xy. These properties feed the bending formulae from Chapter 4.1 and Chapter 4.2.
prereq: You need: the bending stress formula and second moments from Chapter 4.1 and the unsymmetrical stress formula from Chapter 4.2.

sections.h3: The thin-wall assumption and boom idealisation

blocks.text: A wall is thin when its thickness t is much smaller than its length s. Direct stress then varies very little across t, so take it uniform across the thickness. The wall also carries shear mainly along its mid-line. This is the thin-walled assumption. It turns a two-dimensional section into a one-dimensional line of walls. The error is small when t/s is below about 0.1, which covers most aircraft skin and web panels.

Real sections have stringers and skin. Replace the stringers by booms: concentrated areas A_i at their centroid. Keep the skin as effective walls. A wall between two booms can be split into the booms. The usual half-wall rule gives each end boom half the wall area, t s / 2. If several walls meet at a boom, add half of each. A stringer's own area is added once. Two versions are used: fully lumped walls, where walls then carry only shear, or boom-plus-wall, where walls keep their direct-stress area and own second moment. The second version is used below.

items: Boom: concentrated area A_i; carries direct stress.
Wall: thickness t, length s; carries uniform direct stress and shear.

blocks.text: Choose centroidal axes x and y. Let boom i have area A_i at (x_i, y_i). Let a wall have thickness t, length s, and angle θ measured from the x-axis. Sum over every boom and every wall once. The area is:
A = Σ A_i + Σ t s
blocks.where: A_i is boom area (m²); t is wall thickness (m); s is wall length (m); the first sum is over booms, the second over walls.

blocks.text: For second moments, each wall's own term depends on its direction. A wall along x (θ = 0) has its large t s³/12 term about y, not about x. The general thin-wall sums are:
I_xx = Σ A_i y_i² + Σ [ A_w y_c² + (t s³/12) sin²θ + (s t³/12) cos²θ ]
blocks.where: y_i is boom height; A_w = t s is wall area; y_c is the wall centroid's y-coordinate from the section centroid; θ is wall angle from x; the bracket adds the parallel-axis term A_w y_c² and the wall's own I about x. For thin walls the s t³/12 term is often tiny.

blocks.text: I_yy = Σ A_i x_i² + Σ [ A_w x_c² + (t s³/12) cos²θ + (s t³/12) sin²θ ]
blocks.where: x_i is boom horizontal distance; x_c is the wall centroid's x-coordinate; the same wall appears once; bracket adds A_w x_c² and own I about y.

blocks.text: I_xy = Σ A_i x_i y_i + Σ [ A_w x_c y_c + (t s³/12) sinθ cosθ ]
blocks.where: Product second moment; x_c, y_c are wall centroid coordinates; the wall term is zero for walls along x or y; the small s t³/12 product term is neglected.

blocks.text: These wall sums apply to the boom-plus-wall version; in the fully lumped version the wall area is already inside the boom areas. For a rectangular box, four walls suffice: two horizontal and two vertical. Open and closed sections use the same A, I_xx, I_yy and I_xy, so the direct stress from Chapter 4.1 and Chapter 4.2 is the same. Shear flow, shear centre and torsion differ, and are in Unit 5.

The simple answer assumes plane sections stay plane, stress is uniform across each wall, and the material stays linear elastic. Real aircraft panels break these assumptions. Shear lag makes the direct stress uneven across a wide skin panel; booms near a web carry more than booms far away, so an effective width is used. Local buckling makes a thin compressed wall buckle below the yield stress; after buckling it can carry less, and crippling may follow. Plasticity redistributes stress near ultimate load. These effects make the elastic thin-walled answer optimistic for strength and sometimes unsafe for stiffness. Some syllabi call this the applicability of bending theory: use it for quick sizing and preliminary stress, then check with tests, finite elements, or the methods in Unit 6.

spec.title: Idealising a thin-walled box
spec.aria: A five-step flow from the real 100 mm by 60 mm box with 2 mm walls to the summed section properties I_xx and I_yy.

examples.question: A thin-walled rectangular box has mid-line width b = 100 mm, mid-line depth d = 60 mm, and uniform thickness t = 2 mm. The centroidal x-axis is horizontal and the y-axis is vertical. (a) Find I_xx and I_yy. (b) Find the maximum direct stress for M_x = 2 kN·m.
steps: Convert: b = 0.100 m, d = 0.060 m, t = 0.002 m, M_x = 2000 N·m. Top and bottom walls are at y = ±0.030 m. Left and right walls are at x = ±0.050 m.
Two horizontal walls (length b, θ = 0). Each area = b t = 2.00×10⁻⁴ m². Their A y² terms: 2 × 2.00×10⁻⁴ × 0.030² = 3.600×10⁻⁷ m⁴. Their own I_xx: 2 × b t³/12 = 2 × 0.100 × 0.002³/12 = 1.333×10⁻¹⁰ m⁴.
Two vertical walls (length d, θ = 90°). Each area = d t = 1.20×10⁻⁴ m². Their centroids have y = 0, so A y² = 0. Their own I_xx: 2 × t d³/12 = 2 × 0.002 × 0.060³/12 = 7.200×10⁻⁸ m⁴.

For I_yy, horizontal walls have x = 0, so no A x² term. Their own I_yy: 2 × t b³/12 = 2 × 0.002 × 0.100³/12 = 3.3333×10⁻⁷ m⁴. Vertical walls: 2 × (d t)(0.050²) = 6.000×10⁻⁷ m⁴; own I_yy: 2 × d t³/12 = 8.000×10⁻¹¹ m⁴. Total I_yy = 9.3341×10⁻⁷ m⁴.
Maximum stress is at y = 0.030 m: σ = M_x y / I_xx = 2000 × 0.030 / 4.3213×10⁻⁷ = 1.388×10⁸ Pa = 139 MPa.
examples.answer: I_xx = 4.3213×10⁻⁷ m⁴, I_yy = 9.3341×10⁻⁷ m⁴, and the maximum direct stress is 139 MPa.

traps: Using t s³/12 for I_xx when the wall length s runs along x. For a horizontal wall that term belongs to I_yy; its I_xx own term is s t³/12.
Counting a wall shared by two booms twice. Each wall appears once in Σ t s and once in the wall second-moment sum.
Mixing millimetres and metres inside I. Convert b, d, t, x and y to one unit before squaring or cubing.
Dropping the wall's own second moment because it is small. It is small, but the examiner may ask for it and the sum is incomplete without it.
Assuming open and closed sections need different bending formulae. Direct stress is the same; only shear and torsion differ, which is Unit 5.

quiz.q: State the thin-walled assumption in one sentence.
quiz.a: Wall thickness t is much smaller than wall length s, so direct stress is taken uniform across t and shear along the mid-line.

quiz.q: Why does the half-wall rule give half of a wall's area to each end boom?
quiz.a: The wall's direct stress is uniform; splitting its area equally between the two end booms preserves the same total axial force and centroid when the wall is replaced by two concentrated areas.

quiz.q: A vertical wall is 80 mm long and 1.5 mm thick. Find its own I about a horizontal axis through its centroid.
An open C-section and a closed box have the same wall mid-line shape and thickness. Will the bending stress σ = M y / I differ? Explain.
quiz.a: No. For the same A, I_xx, I_yy, I_xy and moment, the direct stress is the same. Open and closed sections differ in shear flow and torsion, not in the direct-stress formula.

quiz.q: A horizontal wall is 120 mm long, 2 mm thick, at y = 25 mm from the centroid. Find its contribution to I_xx, including its own term.
Why is the simple thin-walled bending answer often optimistic for a compressed wing upper panel?
quiz.a: It assumes uniform stress across the wall and no local buckling. Thin compressed walls buckle or cripple before the full stress is reached. Shear lag makes the stress uneven, with higher stress near webs, so the peak stress can exceed the simple beam-theory value; local buckling or crippling also lowers capacity.

quiz.q: Write the thin-walled area formula and define each symbol.
quiz.a: A = Σ A_i + Σ t s; A_i is boom area, t wall thickness, s wall length, sums over booms and walls once.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, a wing box is reduced to a boom-and-panel model for quick sizing, then checked with finite elements that include shear lag and local buckling. Search for shear lag in box beams, effective width stiffened panel, and crippling stress of stringers. Modern topology optimisation uses the same section-property sums inside a sizing loop. Unit 5 takes the shear side; Unit 6 takes buckling and composite panels.
